verses.translation_literal: Praise Yah! Praise God in his holiness, praise him in the vault of his strength.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hallelujah! Let the praise begin, and let it be loud. Lift your voices to God in the place that is his alone, set apart; lift them to him under the great vault of heaven, where his power is stretched out above us all.
verses.directors_commentary:
The book of Psalms ends the way a great ceremony ends, with everyone on their feet. The psalm opens with הַלְלוּ־יָהּ, 'hallelu-Yah', literally a command in the plural: 'praise, all of you, Yah.' Yah is the short form of the divine name, and the KJV's 'Praise ye the Lord' hides both the name and the fact that this is a shout to a crowd. Play it as a call across a courtyard, not a quiet devotion.

The verse sets two stages for praise. 'In his holiness' (בְּקָדְשׁוֹ) can mean his sanctuary, as the KJV and YLT take it, or the holy sphere he occupies; Radak and Metzudat David read it as the world of the angels. 'The vault of his strength' is בִּרְקִיעַ עֻזּוֹ: the rakia is the solid-looking dome of sky from Genesis 1 (a verb that means 'hammered flat', as metal is beaten out), and the KJV's 'firmament' keeps that image without most readers knowing it. Ibn Ezra sees the sky here, and so does Radak. So the two halves cover earth's sanctuary and the heavenly dome: no place is left out. Ibn Ezra reports another view, from Yehuda ha-Levi, that 'his strength' is the Ark. Actors should keep the line wide enough for both.

philological_notes.note: A plural imperative of the root הלל, 'to praise, to boast joyfully in', joined to Yah, the short form of YHWH. The verb is the same one that gives the book its Hebrew title, Tehillim. The word is a command to a group, not a fixed phrase of worship; the KJV's 'Praise ye the Lord' keeps the 'ye' but loses the name.

The rakia is the sky as a hammered-out dome (the verb רקע is to beat out, stamp). It is the word of Genesis 1:6-8. 'Firmament' in KJV comes from the Latin firmamentum, which in turn renders the Greek stereoma, 'something made solid'. Here the dome is the platform on which God's strength is displayed.

verses.translation_literal: Praise him for his mighty deeds, praise him according to the abundance of his greatness.
verses.translation_dramatic: Praise him for what his hand has done, the deeds only he could do. And do not measure out your praise: let it be as large as he is, as full as his greatness, without end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm now moves from where to praise to why. The voice rises: two reasons, each with its own command. 'Mighty deeds' (גְּבוּרֹת) are the acts of a warrior; in Israel's memory they mean the rescue from Egypt and the victories after it. Radak says that this is where God was made great and holy among the nations by redeeming his people. Meiri hears in them the wonders done 'for us, and still done for us always.'

The second colon is a rule for volume. כְּרֹב גֻּדְלוֹ, 'according to the abundance of his greatness', asks that praise be scaled to its object. The KJV's 'excellent greatness' is a mistranslation of the sense: 'excellent' was an old English word for 'surpassing', but today it sounds like a compliment, and the Hebrew has no adjective at all, only rov, 'multitude'. The actor should hear a challenge: you are asked to give a great amount, because he is a great amount. Ibn Ezra reads בגבורותיו as 'recount them': praise as telling the story.

philological_notes.note: 'According to the multitude of'. The noun rov means abundance in number or amount. The preposition kaf sets praise in proportion to greatness, so the line has a sense of measure that the KJV's 'excellent' removes.

verses.translation_literal: Praise him with a blast of shofar; praise him with harp and lyre.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the ram's horn split the air, one raw blast to wake the whole assembly. Praise him! And then let the strings answer it, the harp pouring out its notes, the lyre running beneath them, until the sound is gentle and wide as the blast was sharp.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm now turns from why to how, and it goes through the Temple orchestra instrument by instrument. The actors should not play it as a list but as a procession: each line opens with the same word, hallelu-hu, "praise him", and each instrument is a new voice joining the shout. The first voice is the loudest. The shofar is a ram's horn, not a trumpet; it is not tuned and not musical in our sense. It is the sound of alarm, of the new moon, of the Sinai theophany and of coronation (compare Psalm 47:5 and Psalm 98:6). The Hebrew has a noun, tekaʿ, "a blast", a striking, thrusting word from the verb for blowing and pitching a tent peg; it is a physical act.

The KJV's "the sound of the trumpet" is wrong twice. It turns the shofar into a metal trumpet, which the Hebrew keeps as a separate instrument (chatzotzerah), and it turns a blast into a pleasant "sound". Radak, notably, says the trumpets are included in this praise ("and the trumpets are included in it"), so for him the horn stands for the wind instruments of the Temple. Then the strings enter. The KJV's "psaltery and harp" is an old guess; the nevel was a large, many-stringed instrument and the kinnor the lyre, David's instrument. Ibn Ezra on the nevel adds a concrete detail: it has ten holes. Notice that the order is wind first, strings second: the horn calls to attention, the strings carry the song.

philological_notes.note: The ram's horn, a signal instrument used for alarm, festival and coronation, not a metal trumpet. The Targum renders the phrase 'with the blast of the shofar' (בִּתְקִיעוּתָא דְשׁוֹפָרָא), keeping the Hebrew word rather than a Greek or Latin term for a trumpet. The metal trumpet in the Hebrew Bible is a separate word, חֲצוֹצְרָה. Radak says the trumpets are included in this praise.
A large stringed instrument, probably a harp or a lyre; the KJV's 'psaltery' is the Greek-derived name the Septuagint uses. Ibn Ezra notes it has ten holes (or openings).

verses.translation_literal: Praise him with tambourine and dance; praise him with strings and pipe.
verses.translation_dramatic: Praise him with the drum in the hand and the feet that will not stay still! Praise him, let the dance begin. And let the strings take it up, and under them the pipe, a thin, reedy voice, sweet and piercing, praising him.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the horn and strings the psalm moves to the body. The tof is a small hand drum or frame drum, what the KJV calls a "timbrel", and in Israel it was played by women, as when Miriam leads the women out with tambourines (Exodus 15:20). Pair it with machol, "dance", a circle dance of celebration: the actors should move here. Drum and dance belong together because the beat is for the feet. The Hebrew does not say "timbrel and dance" as two abstractions: they are one scene of a community in motion.

The second line is harder and the KJV hides the difficulty. Minnim is a rare word, and the commentators say frankly that they do not know it: Radak says the instrument is not known to us; Rashi and Metzudat Zion say only that it is a kind of musical instrument; Ibn Ezra reads it as 'many kinds, one tune'; Meiri guesses an organ made of many mixed motions. The KJV's "stringed instruments" is a respectable guess, not a certainty. The ugav, by contrast, is old and well attested. The KJV's "organs" is a serious anachronism: there were no keyboard organs in ancient Israel. The ugav was a pipe or flute, and it appears in Genesis 4:21, where Jubal is the father of all who play the lyre (kinnor) and the pipe (ugav), the first musicians. The psalm closes its orchestra with the oldest instrument in the Bible.

philological_notes.note: A dance, usually a circle dance of celebration, from the root meaning to whirl. It is joined to the tambourine, as in Exodus 15:20 and Judges 11:34. Malbim reads it as a sign that the LORD is the head of the dance, with the righteous around him.

A rare word for a stringed instrument or instruments (also Psalm 45:9 [8]), unclear. Radak says the instrument is not known to us; Rashi calls them kinds of musical instruments; Ibn Ezra reads 'many instruments and one tune'. A gloss of 'strings' is a reasonable guess, not a certainty.
A pipe or flute, not an organ. It is attested in Genesis 4:21, where Jubal is the father of all who play the lyre (kinnor) and the pipe (ugav), and in Job 21:12 and Job 30:31.

verses.translation_literal: Praise him with cymbals of hearing, praise him with cymbals of shouting.
verses.translation_dramatic: Praise him with the clash of the cymbals, a sound you cannot help but hear. Praise him with the cymbals that shout, ringing out over all the rest.
verses.directors_commentary:
The orchestra reaches its loudest moment. The word for cymbals is a plural built from a root that rings, tzil-tzil, and here the sound is its own refrain: tziltzelei shama', tziltzelei teru'ah. The Hebrew literally calls them 'cymbals of hearing' and 'cymbals of shouting', one the cymbals that make themselves heard, the other the ones that cry out. The KJV's 'loud cymbals' and 'high sounding cymbals' makes it two grades of loudness, and the actor should not play a distinction the Hebrew does not give. Rashi and Radak say simply that they are cymbals that make a sound heard far away; Metzudat Zion gives the mechanism: two bronze vessels struck together, as in 1 Chronicles 15:19, and he cites a Mishnah of the Temple service in which a man strikes the cymbal.

What the second set of tziltzelim is differs between the commentators: Meiri and Metzudat Zion think they are trumpets (hatzotzerot), and the parallel with the teru'ah, the war-shout, suggests alarm. Ibn Ezra warns that we cannot know these instruments with certainty, because even the Arab and Edomite sages did not know each other's instruments.

philological_notes.note: A reduplicated form of the root צלל, 'to ring, to tingle', used for cymbals and the like. It is onomatopoeic: the word itself rings. The same repetition in both cola gives the verse its clash.
A noun, 'hearing, sound', not the verb 'to hear'. Rashi observes that it is a noun, like shema', and takes its qamets from the pause accent.

verses.translation_literal: All the breath, let it praise Yah. Praise Yah!
verses.translation_dramatic: And now let everything that draws breath praise the LORD: every living breath, in and out. Hallelujah!
verses.directors_commentary:
The last verse of the Psalter drops the instruments. After all the horns and drums, what is left is the human breath. נְשָׁמָה (neshamah) is the breath of life that God blew into Adam's nostrils in Genesis 2:7; the KJV's 'every thing that hath breath' is right but gets lost in the plural: Hebrew says 'all the breath', one breath that is shared. The line is grammatically 'Let all breath praise Yah', and that means every creature, not only Israel.

Speak this verse more quietly than the rest. After the noise of verse 5 the actor lets the sound fall to a breath, so the psalm ends on the thing it is about. The final הַלְלוּ־יָהּ is the same shout that opened the psalm, and so the book closes the circle. Radak counts thirteen praises in this psalm (twelve commands and the final tehallel), and he sees in them the thirteen attributes of mercy; the Meiri sees here the reward of the world to come. Whichever you choose, the book that began with 'blessed is the man' ends on 'every breath'.

philological_notes.note: The breath of life, the same word as in Genesis 2:7, where God breathes into Adam. A collective singular here, 'all the breath', and so everything alive. Malbim reads it as every single breath of every breathing thing.
